narrative:
The model determined that you have a 61.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. Placing in the 3rd decile is noticeably lower than the average of about 5.8 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker recent academic performance. Your first-year ranking came next in importance and also pulled the outcome toward failure; again, a 3rd-decile placement sits well below the typical 6th-decile level of admitted students. These two academic standing measures outweighed everything else.

Your LSAT score of 36 worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the predicted risk of failure. While this score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, the model still viewed it as a small positive factor.

Taken together, the below-average year-to-year class rankings created a stronger signal of risk than your solid LSAT could offset.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Improving your class rank in future semesters, retaking the LSAT to raise your score, or enrolling in a structured bar-preparation course could meaningfully shift your profile before reapplying. Many students in similar situations have successfully improved these exact areas and gained admission on a later attempt.
